question: Is there anything you can say, sign or point to that takes you out of a court's jurisdiction?
alternates: Can you refuse to consent to a court?
UCC 1-308, gold fringe and the 1871 Act: do any of them work?
premise: Each trick claims a court needs your consent or loses its power by some sign. The documents they cite say otherwise: UCC 1-308 governs reserving rights while performing a commercial contract, the Supreme Court read the 1871 Act as making the District of Columbia a municipal corporation, and a federal court found flag fringe has no legal significance. Courts have rejected the consent and contract arguments in the US, Canada, Australia and New Zealand. The strongest evidence that the arguments always fail is Canadian: 1,089 decisions without a success and 51 refused Supreme Court leave applications; a review of 200+ cases across Australia and New Zealand found the same. US evidence is case law and a federal circuit's summary rejection, not a count, so 'uniformly' is shown for Canada and Australasia and stated by US courts rather than tallied.
whyWatch: Each trick is sold as the loophole judges don't want you to know; the rulings on each one show what happens when someone tries it.
tension: The tricks cite real documents (a commercial code section, an 1871 statute, flag law), but what those documents say is not what the tricks claim.

arc.hook: A defendant writes 'UCC 1-308, without prejudice' under the signature and tells the judge he does not consent.
arc.conflict: Five separate tricks, each pointing to a real document, all aimed at the same thing: a court that has no power over you.
arc.evidence: Read each document for what it says, then the ruling on each trick: Benabe on consent, State v. Smith on 1-308, McCann v. Greenway on the fringe, Metropolitan Railroad on 1871, Bey v. Indiana on statutes as contracts.
arc.resolution: None of the tricks works in any ruling here. The tallies of failure are Canadian and Australasian; in the US the record is a run of rejections, not a count.
arc.takeaway: Jurisdiction comes from law, not from what you sign or say in the room.

questions.question: Is there anything you can say, sign or point to that takes you out of a court's jurisdiction?

central.text: The evidence does not support "Courts have no jurisdiction over you unless you consent or contract with them"

questions.premise: Each trick claims a court needs your consent or loses its power by some sign. The documents they cite say otherwise: UCC 1-308 governs reserving rights while performing a commercial contract, the Supreme Court read the 1871 Act as making the District of Columbia a municipal corporation, and a federal court found flag fringe has no legal significance. Courts have rejected the consent and contract arguments in the US, Canada, Australia and New Zealand. The strongest evidence that the arguments always fail is Canadian: 1,089 decisions without a success and 51 refused Supreme Court leave applications; a review of 200+ cases across Australia and New Zealand found the same. US evidence is case law and a federal circuit's summary rejection, not a count, so 'uniformly' is shown for Canada and Australasia and stated by US courts rather than tallied.
questions.tension: The tricks cite real documents (a commercial code section, an 1871 statute, flag law), but what those documents say is not what the tricks claim.
questions.whyWatch: Each trick is sold as the loophole judges don't want you to know; the rulings on each one show what happens when someone tries it.

arc.hook: A defendant writes 'UCC 1-308, without prejudice' under the signature and tells the judge he does not consent.
arc.conflict: Five separate tricks, each pointing to a real document, all aimed at the same thing: a court that has no power over you.
arc.evidence: Read each document for what it says, then the ruling on each trick: Benabe on consent, State v. Smith on 1-308, McCann v. Greenway on the fringe, Metropolitan Railroad on 1871, Bey v. Indiana on statutes as contracts.
arc.resolution: None of the tricks works in any ruling here. The tallies of failure are Canadian and Australasian; in the US the record is a run of rejections, not a count.
arc.takeaway: Jurisdiction comes from law, not from what you sign or say in the room.

By statute 'national of the United States' includes every citizen and confers no exemption; the Seventh Circuit called the Moorish treaty claim baseless; courts in Australia, Canada and Ohio have rejected the argument that common law or Magna Carta overrides statutes. The limits: the federal rulings against 'state citizen' status come from tax cases, so state jurisdiction is not directly tested, and the evidence on status ID at stops is one FBI report that sellers of immunity ID cards were convicted, not a record of what happened to holders at stops.
questions.tension: Each status borrows something real: the statutory term 'national', old treaties with Morocco, Magna Carta and the common law.
questions.whyWatch: Status paperwork is sold as a way to stop being bound by statutes; the courts that have ruled on each version say what the paperwork does.

arc.hook: A driver hands an officer a state-national ID card and says the statutes do not apply to him.
arc.conflict: Each status points to a real source, a statute, a treaty, a charter, and promoters sell the paperwork.
arc.evidence: 8 USC 1101 and USCIS on who is a national; Bey v. Indiana on the Moorish treaty claim; Australian, Canadian and Ohio courts on Magna Carta and common law; federal tax cases on 'state citizen' status; the FBI on immunity ID cards.
arc.resolution: No court here has accepted any of the four. The federal 'state citizen' rulings are tax cases, and the protection-at-stops claim rests on one report about sellers, so those two parts are settled less directly.
arc.takeaway: A status you declare yourself changes nothing a court will recognise.
